title: Rav Acha bar Abba
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman finds great confusion concerning this Amora, such as we do not find for any other Amora. For in Shabbat 113b, “Rav Acha bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said”; in Kiddushin 81b, that he was Rav Chisda’s father-in-law; in Avodah Zarah 19b, he spoke in Rav Hamnuna’s name; in Zevachim 4b, he raised a difficulty against Rava; in Menachot 5b, he raised a difficulty against Rav Ashi; in Menachot 84b, he raised a difficulty against Rabbah; in Chullin 49a, he sat before Rav Huna; and in Ketubot 44b, he challenges Resh Lakish’s words. Is there greater confusion than this? After great examination Hyman concludes clearly that there was no Amora by this name, and explains each passage in turn.
In Shabbat 113b, the reading of the Rosh and Dikdukei Soferim is “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said,” for as is known he was his student.
In Kiddushin 81b — it is already known that Rav Chanan bar Rava was Rav Chisda’s father-in-law, and not Rav Acha bar Abba.

In Avodah Zarah 19b Hyman proposes “Rav Acha bar Ada said that Rav Hamnuna said that Rav said,” as cited thus in Sukkah 21b. In Zevachim 4b Hyman proposes, as in Dikdukei Soferim, “Rav Ada bar Abba to Rava,” who was his student, as in Bava Batra 22a. In Menachot 5b the reading of Dikdukei Soferim is “Rav Acha bar Rava said to Rav Ashi,” for as is known they were colleagues, and from the word “Rava” came “Rabbi Abba.” In Menachot 84b the reading of Dikdukei Soferim is “Rav Acha bar Huna said to Rabbah,” who was indeed his student. In Chullin 49a the reading of Dikdukei Soferim is “Rav Acha bar Avya or Avira sat before Rabbi Zeira,” and with this we understand well the whole continuation of the Gemara there: Rav Acha bar Avya sat before Rabbi Zeira and said, “Rabbi Malukh said …”; [he replied:] “Is it Malukh the Arab you are citing? He said the halakhah does not follow Rabbi Shimon” — and the Gemara says: How did Rabbi Zeira know this? Because when Rabbi Zeira went up, he found Rav Bivi sitting and saying, “Rabbi Malukh said that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: The halakhah follows Rabbi Shimon.” Rabbi Zeira said to him: “By the Master’s life, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Assi and I visited Rabbi Malukh’s place, and we said to him: Did the Master say the halakhah follows Rabbi Shimon? And he said to us: ‘I said the halakhah does not [follow him].’ ” Hyman infers from the whole continuation of the passage that all this was in the Land of Israel; what connection does it have with Rav Huna, who was in Babylonia, as in our reading? Hyman therefore considers the passage its own guide to interpretation: Rav Acha bar Avya, who was a native of the Land of Israel, said before Rabbi Zeira the words of Rabbi Malukh; but Rabbi Zeira, who had been in Rabbi Malukh’s place and spoke with him face to face, knew the truth of how Rabbi Malukh had said it. He regards this as clear.
For Ketubot 44b Hyman proposes Rav Ada bar Ahavah, as it is there, 40b.

notes.text: Retain the NEGATION אין הלכה and assign the retort to the teacher, as returned Chullin49a shows. Hyman’s proposed Zeira/Avya sequence is distinct from that named Gemara’s Huna/Acha barAbba text. His no-such-Amora conclusion and every emendation remain arguments, not authority deletion. Supplied initial Menachotפס. is read from his later explicit84b, disclosed; האמר is read as the passage, avoiding the draft’s one who says it shows his way.

The consulted Chullin 49a has Acha bar Abba before Huna, followed by Zeira’s report of visiting Malukh and Bivi’s different transmission. Both teacher retort and later quotation retain the negation: the halakhah does not follow Shimon. Hyman proposes a Zeira/Avya sequence and concludes clearly that no Amora bore the heading name; that remains his argument, not authority deletion or a silent replacement of the consulted witness.
